abstract: Resource limitation constrains primary production across vast regions of the global ocean. Diatoms often persist under these conditions, despite their relatively large size and nutrient quotas compared to other phytoplankton phyla. This trend is particularly pronounced in the variable light and iron-depleted waters of the Southern Ocean. Proton-pumping rhodopsins (PPRs) have emerged as an important adaptation underlying this success, allowing diatoms to energetically supplement chlorophyll-based photosynthesis with retinal-based phototrophy, particularly under iron stress. While PPRs are increasingly recognized as a driver of diatom resilience under iron depletion, the extent to which coinciding environmental factors, such as light, shape this adaptation remains unresolved. We performed an in vitro study to investigate how variations in iron availability and light spectra synergistically shape PPR physiology in two ecologically relevant Southern Ocean diatoms: Pseudo-nitzschia subcurvata and Synedra hyperborea. Integrative biochemical and bioinformatic approaches identified two distinct evolutionary strategies for rhodopsin-mediated light acquisition. While P. subcurvata employed a specialist approach with two PPRs utilized under different wavelengths of light (green v. blue/red), S. hyperborea adopted a generalist approach with expression of a single PPR under both light treatments. Structural analyses of PPRs revealed hallmarks consistent with xanthorhodopsins, while coordinated transcriptional and pigment analyses suggest the blue-absorbing xanthophyll diadinoxanthin functions as a secondary light-harvesting chromophore. Collectively, these findings expand the ecological light niche of diatom rhodopsins, reveal previously unrecognized diversity in eukaryotic rhodopsin strategies, and suggest spectral tuning of proton pumping rhodopsins will enhance diatom fitness within the climatically altered light climate of the Southern Ocean.
